# Data available to a strategy

**Generated by `scripts/gen_agent_data.py` from `data/manifest.json` and the run-time types. Do not hand-edit it — your edit will be overwritten and CI will fail first.** Change the code or regenerate after the data extends.

This is the reference for writing a strategy: what you can subscribe to, what fields arrive, and what they mean. `CLAUDE.md` has the repo rules; `docs/data-inventory.md` has the bucket. Neither is this.

## Datasets

| instrument | adapter | sessions | first | last |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ES | **no adapter yet** | 307 | 2025-07-04 | 2026-09-09 |
| NQ | `nq-trades:NQ` | 564 | 2024-07-04 | 2026-09-09 |
| QQQ.OPT | **no adapter yet** | 512 | 2024-07-03 | 2026-07-20 |

Sessions are **assemblable CME sessions**, not files. A session runs 17:00 CT on the previous day to 16:00 CT, so it straddles exactly two UTC-day objects and a session exists only when both are present. File counts are larger and using one as N is wrong.

Coverage is full Globex, not RTH.

## Which split this run serves

- **NQ** — `config/calendars/nq-trades.yaml` **is not written**, so no split is served at all. All 564 assemblable sessions exist, and the adapter raises rather than serving a default.

The train / validation / holdout boundaries are **pre-registered by a human before any outcome is observed**. A split chosen after looking at results is not a pre-registration, so the adapter refuses to invent one — a plausible-looking default would be worse than the error, because every number computed from it would look fine.

Until a calendar is committed, a run either iterates sessions explicitly or uses the smoke path, and nothing it produces is scored.

## Subscriptions

Declare them in `setup(ctx)`, once, before the walk starts. You cannot subscribe later: what data a strategy consumed is part of what it is, and it is recorded. Kinds: `time`, `tick`.

```python
def setup(self, ctx):
    ctx.subscribe("5m")                    # time bars, any interval
    ctx.subscribe("30s")
    ctx.subscribe("1h", emit_empty=True)   # carry the last close through
    ctx.subscribe("tick")                  # every trade event
```

- **Time bars** — any interval (`"250ms"`, `"30s"`, `"5m"`, `"1h"`, or nanoseconds as an int). Anchored to the session open, never to the wall clock, so the first bar of a session starts at its first tick. Empty intervals are skipped unless `emit_empty=True`.
- **Tick events** — `ctx.subscribe("tick")` delivers every trade to `on_tick(ctx)` as `ctx.tick`. This is what volume bars, dollar bars, tick imbalance and every order-flow feature are built from. It is expensive: hundreds of thousands of callbacks per session, and the wall-clock budget makes that an honest cost rather than a hidden one.

Subscribing to the same interval twice returns the same subscription. When several bars close at the same instant you get **one** `on_bars` callback carrying all of them, in `ctx.closed` — never one callback per timeframe, because then the order between them would be a hidden variable that changes results and is recorded nowhere.

## Bar fields

| field | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `sub_id` | `str` | Which subscription produced it (`time:300000000000`, `tick`). One callback can carry bars from several subscriptions. |
| `open_ts` | `int (ns UTC)` | Nanoseconds UTC of the interval's **start**. This is the bar's identity — sort, join and index on it. |
| `close_ts` | `int (ns UTC)` | Nanoseconds UTC of the interval's **end**, which is also the instant you are being called at. Both are carried so nothing downstream has to infer which one it is holding; using `open_ts` as the delivery time is how a join silently takes data from the future. |
| `open` | `float` | First trade price in the interval. |
| `high` | `float` | Highest trade price in the interval. |
| `low` | `float` | Lowest trade price in the interval. |
| `close` | `float` | Last trade price in the interval. |
| `volume` | `int` | Contracts traded in the interval. |
| `tick_count` | `int` | Number of trade events in the interval. Zero only on an `emit_empty=True` bar, where OHLC all carry the previous close forward. |
| `session` | `int` | Session index within the dataset, counting from 0. Bars never span a session boundary. |

`bar.is_empty` is `tick_count == 0`.

**`open_ts` versus `close_ts`.** A bar is stamped with its open and delivered on its close. You are called at `close_ts`; everything in the bar happened in `[open_ts, close_ts)`. Both are on the object so you never have to guess which one a downstream join is using — that guess, made wrong, is lookahead that produces a beautiful equity curve.

## Tick fields

What `on_tick(ctx)` hands you as `ctx.tick`:

| field | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ts` | `int (ns UTC)` | Nanoseconds UTC of the trade. |
| `seq` | `int` | Position in the walk, assigned by the engine. Ticks with equal `ts` keep their feed order through it. |
| `price` | `float` | Trade price. |
| `size` | `int` | Contracts traded. |
| `side` | `Side \| None` | Aggressor. See below — this is the field that gets silently mishandled. |
| `session` | `int` | Session index within the dataset, counting from 0. |

### `side` — the one to get right

The feed's aggressor flag has **three** values, and the third is real:

| feed value | meaning | what you receive |
|---|---|---|
| `B` | bid-initiated | `Side.BUY` (`'buy'`) |
| `A` | ask-initiated | `Side.SELL` (`'sell'`) |
| `N` | **unknown — the feed does not say** | `None` |

`N` must be handled. It must **never** be folded into one side, dropped silently, or defaulted to buy.

It is rare — a few hundred ticks in hundreds of millions; the measured rate for this data is in `docs/datasets/nq-es-qqq.md` — and that rarity is exactly what makes it dangerous. A signed-volume feature that treats `None` as a buy will not show up in any test you write; it will show up as a small, permanent bias in every order-flow number you compute, on data you cannot re-run. Write the branch:

```python
if tick.side is None:
    ...        # decide, explicitly, what unknown aggressor means here
elif tick.side is Side.BUY:
    ...
else:
    ...
```

## Causality

The API is built so lookahead is hard to express rather than merely discouraged, but the rules are worth knowing before you fight them.

- **`setup(ctx)`** runs once, before the walk. It may read the **train split only** — `ctx.ticks()`, `ctx.train_bars(interval)` — to fit parameters. It may not see validation or holdout, and it is the only place a subscription can be declared. Keep whatever you fitted on `self`.
- **`on_bars(ctx)` / `on_tick(ctx)` / `on_fill(ctx)` / `on_lifecycle(ctx)`** run during the walk and see the present instant and the past. `ctx.history(interval)` is closed bars only; indexing at or past the cursor raises `LookaheadError` rather than returning something plausible.
- **Warmup reaches backward, decisions never reach forward.** A warmup of *k* sessions lets features spin up on the *k* sessions before the split starts, so a 20-session moving average is not undefined on day one and the split does not have to donate its own head. Actions taken during warmup are ignored and counted, not executed.
- **Orders are queued.** A callback records intent; the engine applies it after the callback returns. Orders placed on a bar close become eligible on the **next** event, never against the tick that closed the bar (T+1). A context is valid only inside its own callback.

## What is not available

The price source is **trades only**. There is no book and no quote feed, which rules out a family of features that would otherwise look available:

- **No bid/ask, no BBO, no quotes** — so no spread, no mid, no microprice, no quoted-depth imbalance.
- **No order book** — so no queue position, no depth, no book pressure, no cancel/replace flow.
- **No vendor bars.** Bars are built here from trades, so session boundaries and anchoring live in reviewable code rather than in a vendor's convention.

A fill model declares what it requires and the dataset declares what it has; a mismatch is refused at wiring time rather than half-way through a run. Do not write a feature that needs a quote and hope.

## Contract selection

The bucket is requested with `stype_in=PARENT`, which means a `trades` file holds **every** NQ contract — outrights, back months and calendar spreads — not the front month. Choosing one is a research convention, not a fact, so it is written down per session rather than inferred:

- The front month is the **outright** contract with the highest traded volume in that session. Spreads (`NQU5-NQZ5`) are separate instruments in the same file and are excluded, so they cannot win the comparison.
- The choice is recorded for every session in `data/nq-contract-selection.json`, so a roll is visible as data instead of being read off a chart, and a wrong rule shows up as a contract that changes on the wrong day or flickers back and forth.
- 564 sessions recorded, across 9 contracts (NQH5, NQH6, NQM5, NQM6, NQU4, NQU5, NQU6, NQZ4, NQZ5), with 8 roll(s) and no flicker — the chosen contract never returns to one it has left.
- **`near_roll`** is set on 39 of them. share_of_session_volume < 0.9: the chosen contract had a real competitor in that session. Every flagged session is within four calendar days of a roll. It is a flag, not an exclusion: decide for yourself whether your feature survives a session where two contracts split the volume, and say which you did. A result that depends on those 39 sessions is telling you about the roll convention, not about the market.

Each row carries `session`, `instrument_id`, `raw_symbol`, `volume`, `trades`, `share_of_session_volume`, `near_roll` and the `rule` that chose it.
